questions.prompt: Where is the puck at this freeze?

questions.prompt: Which two pieces of information help before this pickup?

options.text: Whether D2 can offer an outlet

questions.explanation: Pressure and support shape the first read; they do not guarantee a specific pass.

questions.prompt: Order one preparation routine for this rim.

options.text: Control the puck and reassess the outlet

questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine; scanning may happen repeatedly.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a pickup position that preserves a view of Gold 1.
questions.explanation: A position inside the rim can allow a check of pressure. Another angle may suit the puck’s actual travel.

questions.prompt: Suppose Gold 1 now reaches the wall first. What deserves a fresh look?

options.text: Contain and support rather than assume you own the puck
Continue the planned outlet as though possession is secure
Leave for a rush before seeing the puck

questions.explanation: A contested pickup changes the job. The exact response depends on support and reach.

questions.prompt: What would you look at twice while retrieving this rim?
questions.explanation: Explain how the forechecker or outlet may move between the first scan and the pickup.

questions.prompt: Which new fact would make the planned pickup less certain?

options.text: Gold 1 reaches the rim before YOU
W stays higher in the zone

questions.explanation: Gold 1 reaching the rim changes possession risk, so YOU must protect and support; if YOU arrives first with control, the outlet scan returns.

questions.prompt: Which two words would make the next call useful?

options.text: Call for a pass without naming a lane

questions.explanation: A pressure-side call and support status give teammates actionable information; a vague pass call does not say what changed.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an approach angle that keeps the loose rim and Gold 1 in view.
questions.explanation: The offset approach preserves a view of both puck and forechecker; if Gold 1 crosses the lane, slow and support rather than reaching blind.

questions.prompt: How would you decide whether to collect or contain at the rim?
questions.explanation: Compare who can reach the puck, Gold 1’s route and D2’s support before committing; if the opponent arrives first, contain and wait for help.

questions.prompt: Select two checks before using the permitted reverse.

Whether pressure can reach the reverse route

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible reverse decision.

options.text: Use the reverse only if that route remains available

questions.explanation: The routine supports a decision, not an automatic reverse every time pressure appears.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example spot for protecting possession while looking toward D2.
questions.explanation: A tighter position near the back of the net can change the approach angle. Actual goalie and defender locations still matter.

questions.prompt: If D2 is closely marked before you release, what is sensible?

options.text: Reverse automatically because it was the original plan
Pass through D2’s marker without checking

questions.explanation: A closed second option means another read is needed; holding may be useful if possession can be protected.

questions.prompt: Why is “the first outlet is closed” insufficient by itself to choose a reverse?
questions.explanation: A different lane and a prepared receiver must also exist. Mention pressure on D2 or time to protect the puck.

questions.prompt: What does Gold 1’s position between YOU and W change?

options.text: The direct W outlet is restricted
The puck is already in the neutral zone

questions.explanation: Gold 1 occupies the direct lane to W, so that pass needs a different angle or protection; if Gold 1 moves away, recheck W.

questions.prompt: Which two details should accompany a reverse call?

questions.explanation: The behind-net position can change Gold 1’s angle and keep D2 in view; if Gold 1 follows, protect before choosing the reverse.

questions.prompt: Why does a closed strong-side outlet permit a reverse without requiring it?
questions.explanation: The closure removes one lane while D2’s side and pressure determine whether the reverse helps; if the reverse is covered too, protect or wait.

questions.explanation: Coming off the boards can separate the passing route from Gold 1. Check C’s space rather than crowding it.

questions.explanation: The inward angle steps off Gold 1’s direct route and gives D1 a short option; if Gold 1 follows, C may become the next outlet.

questions.prompt: How can movement help D1 even if the puck goes to C?
questions.explanation: Stepping off the direct lane can pull Gold 1 and open C or D1’s next route; if the defender ignores you, D1 can use the space you created.

questions.prompt: What is YOU’s stated first job?

questions.prompt: Which two cues tell YOU whether to stay underneath W?

questions.prompt: Move YOU below and inside W to present the assigned short outlet.
questions.explanation: The lower-inside spot gives W a short lane away from Gold 1; if W gains space, widen to support the next play.

questions.prompt: What would make you leave the short-outlet position?
questions.explanation: Leave when W has secure control and a better visible lane opens, or when pressure closes your route; if W remains pinned, stay available.

questions.explanation: The role is stated in the briefing and is not inferred from a system name.

questions.prompt: What two features could make F2’s option different from F1’s?

options.text: A position closer to Navy’s net

questions.explanation: Different depth and angle can create another choice; a defender may still close it.

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible regroup support routine.

questions.prompt: Why can two forwards at the same height make D1’s job harder?

questions.prompt: What did the coach ask YOU to provide?

questions.prompt: Move YOU below F1 into the coach-assigned middle support pocket.
questions.explanation: The lower-middle spot separates YOU from F1 and gives D1 a safer connection; if Gold 1 follows, preserve the lane behind the pressure.

questions.prompt: Why can two players at the same height make D1’s reset harder?
questions.explanation: They present one predictable line, allowing one defender to cover both, while different heights create a forward and backward choice; if one lane closes, the other can remain.
